Answer: <0 or 1>

prediction.raw: <1> **YTA (Yes, you're the asshole)**. Here's why: ### **Key Reason: "Open invitation" ≠ "No need to communicate details"** - An "open invitation" means **no one is excluded**, but it **does not mean you can assume people know about the event**. - You explicitly stated: "Everyone in the family that can attend is always welcome." **"Always welcome" requires proactively sharing the event details** (date, time, location) with *every* family member. - **Social media posts are unreliable** for critical communication. If your wife only posted a *after* the event (to "honor her dad"), that’s **too late** for the unrepresented family to attend. Relying on "they should know" or "they check social media" is passive and inconsiderate. - **"They have been every other year" is irrelevant**. People’s schedules change, they might assume the event is canceled, or they might not see your post. **It’s the host’s responsibility to ensure all expected attendees are informed**. ### **Why this is AITA behavior** - **You placed the burden on others** to "take initiative" to attend a event they weren’t told about. - **You dismissed their feelings** (" flew off the handle") without considering that ** not being informed is a valid reason to feel excluded**. - **"I didn’t get an invite and I showed up" proves your point is flawed**. If *you* didn’t get an invite but showed up (because you knew about it), that means **you had prior knowledge** (e.g., a group text, family chat, or verbal reminder). **Why didn’t you extend that same courtesy to the unrepresented family?** - **This is a basic courtesy issue**. For a family event tied to a deceased loved one (especially one where the mother-in-law pays), **omitting a family member from communication is hurtful and inconsiderate**. ### **What you should have done** - **Directly message all family members** (via text, call, or group chat) with: > "Annual celebration for Dad on March 31st at [restaurant]! Mom’s treating, all welcome. Let me know if you can make it!" - **Follow up** a few days before if no one responds. - **Never rely on social media** for event details— it’s for *after* the fact (e.g., "We had a great time honoring Dad today!"). ### **Final verdict** You’re not "wrong" for wanting to honor your father-in-law, but **your approach was thoughtless**. "Open invitation" doesn’t mean "no one needs to be told it’s happening." **Assuming others will figure it out is AITA behavior**. Next time, *communicate*— it’s the bare minimum of respect. **YTA (1)**. *(P.S. The unrepresented family’s reaction may seem " over the top," but their frustration is valid. A simple text would have prevented this entirely.)*
